newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Heavy fighting in Zaire as world readies force.
newsitem.headline: Heavy fighting in Zaire as world readies force.

text.p: Heavy fighting flared around the town of Goma in eastern Zaire on Thursday between rebels and their Hutu foes holed up in the teeming refugee camp of Mugunga.

As the world readied to intervene in Central Africa after almost four weeks of crisis, firing from mortar, anti-aircraft and machineguns reverberated around the camp about 10 km (six miles) west of the rebel-held town on Rwanda's border.

The fighting erupted as news broke in Goma that the multinational force being set up to venture into in eastern Zaire will not try to disarm the Hutu fighters when they bring aid to the refugees displaced by the Tutsi rebellion.
Goma residents said they believed the rebels were trying to take on the Hutu fighters before the arrival of the Canadian-led force, with a powerful U.S. military contingent, in a few days.
The United States and Britain have cautiously agreed to send troops, but with memories of previous botched U.N. missions still fresh, they want strictly defined goals.
A U.S. assessment team of more than 40 arrived in the Rwandan capital Kigali from Uganda on Thursday to check out conditions on the ground for logistical support.

"We are here to conduct an initial assessment for a possible mission... either unilateral or multilateral," Major-General Edward Smith, commander of the South European Task Force based at Vicenza in Italy, told reporters.
France, Spain and several African countries, including South Africa, have already said they will send troops.

The French, deeply distrusted by Tutsis in the region for their financial and military support to Rwanda's now-discredited former Hutu government, said on Thursday they hoped the first troops would be in Zaire by the weekend.

The world community is eager to avoid a re-run of 1994 when it effectively fed and gave sanctuary to many of those responsible for the slaughter of an estimated 800,000 people, mainly Tutsis, in Rwanda earlier that year.
At the same time they are keen to learn the lessons of U.N. operations in Somalia, where the U.S. suffered high casualties in a fruitless attempt to apprehend one warlord.

White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry said the U.S. commitment, expected to last about four months, involved sending 1,000 ground troops to Zaire. An additional 2,000 to 3,000 American troops would go to nearby countries to help with support activities, the Pentagon said.

"The president has decided that the United States is willing, in principle, to participate in a limited fashion in this mission as long as certain conditions are stipulated to," McCurry told a White House briefing.
McCurry said the mission would have to be very clearly defined and would not try to disarm militants.
Canadian Army Lt. Gen. Maurice Baril will lead the multilateral force to bring in aid to desperate Rwandan and Burundian Hutus, some cut off from help since local Tutsis rebelled a month ago.

"(U.S.) troops could be flowing into place sometime next week," said a senior Pentagon official, adding that the 1,000 troops in Zaire would include about 600 elite paratroopers from the U.S. 508th Airborne Infantry Regiment based at Vicenza.
Defence Secretary William Perry told reporters the United States planned to send about 1,000 troops to Goma to secure and run the airport, the key centre for distributing relief.
They will also set up a protected corridor about three km (two miles) long from Goma to nearby Rwanda to allow refugees to return to Rwanda if the voluntarily chose to do so.

A United Nations envoy negotiating a mandate for the force with Rwanda and Zaire, whose army is battling Rwandan-backed Tutsi rebels, said it was unclear how the Canadian-led troops could handle armed Hutus using refugees as a screen.
